lessons.title: Exercise 9.8
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A cubical pit of side 12 m holds 12³ = 1728 m³ of soil; three trucks carrying 19.2 m³ each move 57.6 m³ per turn, so 30 turns are needed.
  • Weight = volume × weight per unit volume: a metal cube of side 4.5 cm has volume 91.125 cm³ and weighs 91.125 × 16 = 1458 g.
  • Cost by volume = volume × rate: a stage 8 m × 5 m × 1 m = 40 m³ costs 40 × Rs.1500 = Rs.60,000.
  • Cylinders of equal height have volumes in the ratio of the squares of their diameters: diameters 1.2 m and 1.6 m give ratio 9 : 16.
  • Digging a well of diameter 2 m and depth 21 m removes π × 1² × 21 = 66 m³ of earth, costing 66 × Rs.300 = Rs.19,800.
  • A cone-shaped minaret 12 dm high with diameter 14 dm has volume (1/3) × (22/7) × 7² × 12 = 616 dm³.
  • A football of radius 10.5 cm has volume (4/3) × (22/7) × 10.5³ = 4851 cm³.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. A sewerage pit, having the shape of a cube, was dug with a side measuring 12 m. In how many turns, three trucks will be able to take away the soil if 19.2 m³ soil can be loaded on one truck.

Ans: Volume of the pit = 12³ = 1728 m³
Soil taken by three trucks in one turn = 3 × 19.2 = 57.6 m³
Number of turns = 1728 / 57.6 = 30 turns

Q: Q2. A solid cube is made of a metal. What will be volume of the cube if one of its sides is 4(1/2) cm. Find its weight if 1 cm³ of the metal weighs 16 gram.

Ans: Volume of the cube = (side)³ = (4(1/2))³ = 4.5³ = 91.125 cm³
Weight = 91.125 × 16 = 1458 g

Q: Q3. Tariq bought a piece of wood 2 m long, 35 cm wide and 25 cm thick. What will it cost him if the rate of wood is Rs.24000 per m³?

Ans: Volume of the wood = 2 m × 0.35 m × 0.25 m = 0.175 m³
Cost = 0.175 × Rs.24000 = Rs.4200

Q: Q4. Find the total expenditure on constructing a stage for a function at Rs.1500 per m³, if the stage is 8 m long, 5 m wide and 1 m high.

Ans: Volume of the stage = 8 × 5 × 1 = 40 m³
Total expenditure = 40 × Rs.1500 = Rs.60,000

Q: Q5. Two cylindrical drums of kerosene oil have the same height of 1.5 m and are made of same material. Their diameters are 1.2 m and 1.6 m. Find the ratio of their volumes.

Ans: The heights are equal, so the volumes are in the ratio of the squares of the radii (diameters).
Ratio = (1.2)² : (1.6)² = 1.44 : 2.56 = 9 : 16

Q: Q6. What will be the cost of digging a 21 m deep well having a diameter of 2 m at Rs.300 per m³?

Ans: Radius = 2/2 = 1 m. Volume of earth dug = πr²h = (22/7) × 1² × 21 = 66 m³
Cost = 66 × Rs.300 = Rs.19,800

Q: Q7. A cone shaped minaret is 12 dm high and has a diameter of 14 dm. Find its volume.

Ans: Radius = 14/2 = 7 dm. Volume of a cone = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3) × (22/7) × 7² × 12 = 616 dm³

Q: Q8. Find the volume of a decorative cap, having a shape of cone, with radius of 2.1 cm and height of 10 cm.

Ans: Volume = (1/3) × (22/7) × 2.1² × 10 = (1/3) × (22/7) × 4.41 × 10 = 46.2 cm³

Q: Q9. Find the volume of a children's football with radius of 10.5 cm.

Ans: Volume of a sphere = (4/3)πr³ = (4/3) × (22/7) × 10.5³ = (4/3) × (22/7) × 1157.625 = 4851 cm³

Q: Q10. Dome of a masjid is hemisphere in shape. Find its volume to the nearest tenths if its diameter is 2.1 m.

Ans: Radius = 2.1/2 = 1.05 m. Volume of a hemisphere = (2/3)πr³ = (2/3) × (22/7) × 1.05³ = (2/3) × (22/7) × 1.157625 = 2.425 m³ (about 2.4 m³ to the nearest tenth)

Q: Q11. A metallic sphere is erected in a fountain. Find its volume when its diameter is 5(1/4) dm.

Ans: Radius = (5(1/4))/2 = 21/8 dm. Volume = (4/3) × (22/7) × (21/8)³ = (4/3) × (22/7) × (9261/512) = 606(3/8) dm³

mcqs.q: A cubical sewerage pit has side 12 m. Three trucks together carry 19.2 m³ of soil per truck in one turn. In how many turns can they take away all the soil?
mcqs.why: Volume of the pit = (side)³ = 12³ = 12 × 12 × 12 = 1728 m³. Soil taken by three trucks in one turn = 3 × 19.2 = 57.6 m³. Number of turns = 1728 / 57.6 = 30 turns.

mcqs.q: A solid metal cube has side 4(1/2) cm. Find its weight if 1 cm³ of the metal weighs 16 grams.
Tariq bought a piece of wood 2 m long, 35 cm wide and 25 cm thick. What will it cost at Rs.24000 per m³?
mcqs.why: Convert to metres: width = 0.35 m and thickness = 0.25 m. Volume of the wood = 2 × 0.35 × 0.25. First 2 × 0.35 = 0.7, then 0.7 × 0.25 = 0.175 m³. Cost = 0.175 × Rs.24000 = Rs.4200.

mcqs.q: Find the total expenditure on constructing a stage 8 m long, 5 m wide and 1 m high at Rs.1500 per m³.
mcqs.why: Volume of the stage = length × width × height = 8 × 5 × 1 = 40 m³. Total expenditure = 40 × Rs.1500 = Rs.60,000.

mcqs.q: Two cylindrical drums have the same height and diameters 1.2 m and 1.6 m. Find the ratio of their volumes.
mcqs.why: The heights are equal, so the volumes are in the ratio of the squares of the radii (diameters). Ratio = (1.2)² : (1.6)² = 1.44 : 2.56. Dividing both by 0.16: 1.44/0.16 : 2.56/0.16 = 9 : 16.

mcqs.q: What will be the cost of digging a well 21 m deep having diameter 2 m, at Rs.300 per m³? (Take π = 22/7)
mcqs.why: Radius = 2/2 = 1 m. Volume of earth dug = πr²h = (22/7) × 1² × 21 = 22 × 3 = 66 m³. Cost = 66 × Rs.300 = Rs.19,800.

mcqs.q: A cone-shaped minaret is 12 dm high and has a diameter of 14 dm. Find its volume. (Take π = 22/7)
Find the volume of a cone-shaped decorative cap with radius 2.1 cm and height 10 cm. (Take π = 22/7)
Find the volume of a children's football with radius 10.5 cm. (Take π = 22/7)
A metallic sphere is erected in a fountain. Find its volume when its diameter is 5(1/4) dm. (Take π = 22/7)
mcqs.why: Radius = diameter/2 = (21/4)/2 = 21/8 dm. Volume of a sphere = (4/3)πr³ = (4/3) × (22/7) × (21/8)³ = (88/21) × (9261/512) = 4851/64 ≈ 75.80 dm³. Note: the printed value 606(3/8) dm³ is obtained by wrongly using the diameter 21/4 as the radius; with the correct radius 21/8 the volume is about 75.80 dm³.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.9
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Area of a right-angled triangle = (1/2) × base × altitude: legs 3 cm and 4 cm give 6 cm².
  • Hero's formula with sides 9 cm, 10 cm, 17 cm: s = 18 and area = √(18 × 9 × 8 × 1) = √1296 = 36 cm².
  • A rectangle with diagonal 13 cm and one side 5 cm has other side √(169 − 25) = 12 cm and area 60 cm².
  • A square whose diagonal is 5√2 cm has side 5 cm and area 25 cm².
  • Volume of a cylinder = πr²h: radius 4 cm and height 21 cm give 1056 cm³; a cone of radius 7 cm and height 24 cm gives (1/3)πr²h = 1232 cm³.
  • Volume of a hemisphere of radius 3 cm = (2/3)π(3³) = 18π cm³; volume of a sphere of radius 9 cm = (4/3)π(9³) = 972π cm³.
  • Composite solids are split into cuboids or found by subtraction: an L-shaped solid gives 24000 cm³ and a C-shaped solid gives 7000 − 3250 = 3750 cm³.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1 (i). Find the area of the shape: a right-angled triangle with legs 3 cm and 4 cm.

Ans: The figure is a right-angled triangle with base 3 cm and altitude 4 cm.
Area = (1/2) × base × altitude = (1/2) × 3 × 4 = 6 cm²

Q: Q1 (ii). A triangle with sides 9 cm, 10 cm and 17 cm.

Ans: By Hero's formula with sides 9, 10, 17: s = (9 + 10 + 17)/2 = 18
Area = √(18 × 9 × 8 × 1) = √1296 = 36 cm²

Q: Q1 (iii). A rectangle with diagonal 13 cm and one side 5 cm.

Ans: The diagonal (13 cm) divides the rectangle into two right triangles; by Pythagoras theorem the other side = √(13² − 5²) = √144 = 12 cm.
Area = 12 × 5 = 60 cm²

Q: Q1 (iv). A square of side 5.5 cm.

Ans: Area of a square = (side)² = 5.5² = 30.25 cm²

Q: Q1 (v). A parallelogram with base 13 cm and altitude 8.5 cm.

Ans: Area of a parallelogram = base × altitude = 13 × 8.5 = 110.5 cm²

Q: Q1 (vi). A square whose diagonal is 5√2 cm.

Ans: The diagonal of the square is 5√2 cm, so its side = 5√2/√2 = 5 cm.
Area = 5² = 25 cm²

Q: Q2 (i). Find the volume of the figure: a cube of edge 8 cm.

Ans: Volume of a cube = (edge)³ = 8³ = 512 cm³

Q: Q2 (ii). A cuboid 20 cm × 12 cm × 8 cm.

Ans: Volume of a cuboid = length × breadth × height = 20 × 12 × 8 = 1920 cm³

Q: Q2 (iii). A cylinder of radius 4 cm and height 21 cm.

Ans: Volume of a cylinder = πr²h = (22/7) × 4² × 21 = (22/7) × 16 × 21 = 1056 cm³

Q: Q2 (iv). A cone of radius 7 cm and height 24 cm.

Ans: Volume of a cone = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3) × (22/7) × 7² × 24 = 1232 cm³

Q: Q2 (v). A hemisphere of radius 3 cm.

Ans: Volume of a hemisphere = (2/3)πr³ = (2/3) × π × 3³ = 18π cm³

Q: Q2 (vi). A sphere of radius 9 cm.

Ans: Volume of a sphere = (4/3)πr³ = (4/3) × π × 9³ = 972π cm³

Q: Q2 (vii). An L-shaped solid: overall height 60 cm, overall width 80 cm, inner step 60 cm long and 40 cm high, depth 10 cm.

Ans: The solid is L-shaped. Split it into two cuboids: the vertical part (80 − 60) cm wide, 60 cm high and the horizontal part 60 cm wide, (60 − 40) cm high, both 10 cm deep.
Volume = [20 × 60 + 60 × 20] × 10 = [1200 + 1200] × 10 = 24000 cm³

Q: Q2 (viii). A C-shaped solid: outer block 20 cm wide, 35 cm high, 10 cm deep, with an inner notch 25 cm high and 13 cm deep.

Ans: The solid is C-shaped: a block 20 cm × 35 cm × 10 cm with a rectangular notch 13 cm × 25 cm × 10 cm removed.
Volume = 20 × 35 × 10 − 13 × 25 × 10 = 7000 − 3250 = 3750 cm³

mcqs.q: Find the area of a right-angled triangle with legs 3 cm and 4 cm.
mcqs.why: Area = (1/2) × base × altitude = (1/2) × 3 × 4. First 3 × 4 = 12, then (1/2) × 12 = 6 cm².

mcqs.q: Find the area of a triangle with sides 9 cm, 10 cm and 17 cm.
Find the area of a rectangle with diagonal 13 cm and one side 5 cm.
mcqs.why: The diagonal divides the rectangle into two right triangles; by Pythagoras theorem the other side = √(13² − 5²) = √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12 cm. Area = 12 × 5 = 60 cm².

mcqs.q: Find the area of a square of side 5.5 cm.
mcqs.why: Area of a square = (side)² = 5.5² = 5.5 × 5.5 = 30.25 cm².

mcqs.q: Find the area of a parallelogram with base 13 cm and altitude 8.5 cm.
mcqs.why: Area of a parallelogram = base × altitude = 13 × 8.5. First 13 × 8 = 104, then 13 × 0.5 = 6.5, so the area = 104 + 6.5 = 110.5 cm².

mcqs.q: Find the area of a square whose diagonal is 5√2 cm.
mcqs.why: The diagonal of a square = side × √2, so side = 5√2/√2 = 5 cm. Area = (side)² = 5² = 25 cm².

mcqs.q: Find the volume of a cube of edge 8 cm.
mcqs.why: Volume of a cube = (edge)³ = 8³ = 8 × 8 × 8. First 8 × 8 = 64, then 64 × 8 = 512 cm³.

mcqs.q: Find the volume of a cylinder of radius 4 cm and height 21 cm. (Take π = 22/7)
mcqs.why: Volume of a cylinder = πr²h = (22/7) × 4² × 21. First 4² = 16, then 21/7 = 3, so the volume = 22 × 16 × 3 = 1056 cm³.

mcqs.q: Find the volume of a cone of radius 7 cm and height 24 cm. (Take π = 22/7)
mcqs.why: Volume of a cone = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3) × (22/7) × 7² × 24. First 7² = 49 and 49/7 = 7, then 22 × 7 × 24 = 3696, and finally (1/3) × 3696 = 1232 cm³.

mcqs.q: An L-shaped solid (split into parts 20 cm × 60 cm and 60 cm × 20 cm, depth 10 cm) has what volume?
mcqs.why: Split the L-shape into two cuboids, both 10 cm deep: the vertical part (80 − 60) = 20 cm wide and 60 cm high, and the horizontal part 60 cm wide and (60 − 40) = 20 cm high. Volume = [20 × 60 + 60 × 20] × 10 = [1200 + 1200] × 10 = 2400 × 10 = 24000 cm³.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 9
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Pythagoras theorem: in △PQR with ∠Q = 90°, PQ = 12 cm and QR = 5 cm, the hypotenuse PR = 13 cm.
  • Hero's formula uses s = (a + b + c)/2; for a = 5, b = 3, c = 6, s = 7, and Area = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)).
  • Area of four walls of a room = 2(l + b) × h.
  • Area of a circle = πr²: radius 6 cm gives 36π cm²; the area enclosed by concentric circles of radii 7 cm and 5 cm is 24π cm².
  • A semi-circle of area 77 cm² has radius 7 cm, since (1/2) × (22/7) × r² = 77 gives r² = 49.
  • Volume formulas: cuboid = (area of base) × height, cylinder = πr²h, cone = (1/3) × (area of base × height), hemisphere = (2/3)πr³, sphere = (4/3)πr³.
  • A sphere of volume 288π cm³ has radius 6 cm, since (4/3)πr³ = 288π gives r³ = 216.

mcqs.q: In △PQR, m∠Q = 90°, mPQ = 12 cm, mQR = 5 cm, then mPR =
mcqs.why: Since ∠Q = 90°, PR is the hypotenuse. By Pythagoras theorem: (mPR)² = (mPQ)² + (mQR)² = 12² + 5² = 144 + 25 = 169. Taking the square root: mPR = √169 = 13 cm.

mcqs.q: In △KLM, m∠L = 90°, mKM = 20 cm, mKL = 12 cm, then mLM =
mcqs.why: KM is the hypotenuse (20 cm) since ∠L = 90°. By Pythagoras theorem: (mLM)² = (mKM)² − (mKL)² = 20² − 12² = 400 − 144 = 256. Taking the square root: mLM = √256 = 16 cm.

mcqs.q: In △ABC, m∠A = 90°, mAB = 15 cm, mBC = 25 cm, then mCA =
mcqs.why: BC is the hypotenuse (25 cm) since ∠A = 90°. By Pythagoras theorem: (mCA)² = (mBC)² − (mAB)² = 25² − 15² = 625 − 225 = 400. Taking the square root: mCA = √400 = 20 (in the same unit as the given sides).

mcqs.q: In △ABC, a = 5, b = 3, c = 6, then s =
mcqs.why: s is the semi-perimeter: s = (a + b + c)/2 = (5 + 3 + 6)/2 = 14/2 = 7.

mcqs.q: If the sides of a △ABC are a, b, c and s = (a + b + c)/2, then area of △ABC =
mcqs.why: Hero's formula gives the area of a triangle from its three sides: Area = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)), where s = (a + b + c)/2 is the semi-perimeter. The square root and the factor s must both be present, and each bracket subtracts one side from s.

mcqs.q: Base of a triangle is 8 cm, its altitude is 3 cm, its area =
mcqs.why: Area of a triangle = (1/2) × base × altitude = (1/2) × 8 × 3. First 8 × 3 = 24, then (1/2) × 24 = 12 cm².

mcqs.q: Area of an equilateral triangle is 4√3 cm². Its side =
mcqs.why: Area of an equilateral triangle = (√3/4) × a², so 4√3 = (√3/4) × a². Then a² = 4√3 × 4/√3 = 16. Taking the square root: a = √16 = 4 cm.

mcqs.q: Area of four walls of a room =
mcqs.why: The four walls form two pairs of rectangles: two walls of l × h and two of b × h. Total area = 2lh + 2bh = 2(l + b) × h, where l is the length, b the breadth and h the height of the room.

mcqs.q: Radius of a circle is 6 cm, its area =
mcqs.why: Area of a circle = πr² = π × 6² = π × 36 = 36π cm².

mcqs.q: Area enclosed by two circles having radii 7 cm and 5 cm, is
mcqs.why: Area enclosed by two concentric circles = π(R² − r²) = π × (7² − 5²) = π × (49 − 25) = 24π cm².

mcqs.q: Volume of a cube is 512 mm³. Its edge =
mcqs.why: Volume of a cube = (edge)³, so edge = ∛512. Since 8 × 8 × 8 = 512, the edge = 8 mm.

mcqs.q: Volume of a right circular cylinder =
mcqs.why: A cylinder's volume is the area of its circular base multiplied by its height: Volume = πr² × h = πr²h, where r is the radius of the base and h is the height.

mcqs.q: Radius of the base of a cylinder is 2 cm and height is 10 cm, its volume =
mcqs.why: Volume of a cylinder = πr²h = π × 2² × 10. First 2² = 4, then 4 × 10 = 40, so the volume = 40π cm³.

mcqs.q: Volume of a hemisphere =
mcqs.why: A hemisphere is half of a sphere. Volume of a sphere = (4/3)πr³, so volume of a hemisphere = (1/2) × (4/3)πr³ = (2/3)πr³.

mcqs.q: Volume of a sphere is 288π cm³. Its radius =
mcqs.why: Volume of a sphere = (4/3)πr³, so 288π = (4/3)πr³. Then r³ = 288π × 3/(4π) = 864/4 = 216. Taking the cube root: r = ∛216 = 6 cm, since 6 × 6 × 6 = 216.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.1
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A point is written as an ordered pair (x, y): the first number is the x-coordinate (horizontal distance from the origin) and the second is the y-coordinate (vertical distance).
  • Points on the x-axis have y-coordinate 0, e.g. I(3, 0) and H(−4, 0); points on the y-axis have x-coordinate 0, e.g. T(0, 9) and E(0, −3).
  • Quadrant I: x > 0, y > 0; Quadrant II: x < 0, y > 0; Quadrant III: x < 0, y < 0; Quadrant IV: x > 0, y < 0.
  • A point with y-coordinate 0 lies on the x-axis and a point with x-coordinate 0 lies on the y-axis — such points are in no quadrant.
  • Distance formula between (x1, y1) and (x2, y2): d = √((x2 − x1)² + (y2 − y1)²).
  • Using the distance formula: distance between (3, 7) and (−5, 1) is 10; between (−7, 2) and (5, 7) is 13; between (−4, 12) and (6, −12) is 26.
  • To plot a point, move along the x-axis by the x-coordinate (right if positive, left if negative), then parallel to the y-axis by the y-coordinate (up if positive, down if negative).

Solved Exercises

Ans: Reading the horizontal (x) and vertical (y) distances from the origin in the figure: A is 10 units left and 2 units up: A(−10, 2)

Q: Q2 (i). Determine the x and y coordinates of the point A(−2, 5) and then plot the point.

Ans: In the ordered pair (x, y), the first number is the x-coordinate and the second is the y-coordinate.
A(−2, 5): x = −2, y = 5. Plotted 2 units left of the origin and 5 units up (Quadrant II).

Q: Q2 (ii). B(3, 0)

Ans: B(3, 0): x = 3, y = 0. The point lies on the x-axis, 3 units to the right of the origin.

Q: Q2 (iii). C(6, −7)

Ans: C(6, −7): x = 6, y = −7. Plotted 6 units right and 7 units down (Quadrant IV).

Q: Q2 (iv). D(−4, −2)

Ans: D(−4, −2): x = −4, y = −2 (Quadrant III).

Q: Q2 (v). E(0, −3)

Ans: E(0, −3): x = 0, y = −3. The point lies on the y-axis, 3 units below the origin.

Q: Q2 (vi). F(8, 4)

Ans: F(8, 4): x = 8, y = 4 (Quadrant I).

Q: Q2 (vii). G(0, 6)

Ans: G(0, 6): x = 0, y = 6. The point lies on the y-axis, 6 units above the origin.

Q: Q2 (viii). H(−4, 0)

Ans: H(−4, 0): x = −4, y = 0. The point lies on the x-axis, 4 units to the left of the origin.

Q: Q3 (i). In which quadrant is the point (7, √5) lying?

Ans: Both coordinates are positive (x = 7 > 0, y = √5 > 0), so the point lies in Quadrant I.

Q: Q3 (ii). (5, 9.5)

Ans: Both coordinates positive: Quadrant I.

Q: Q3 (iii). (√2, −4.1)

Ans: x = √2 > 0, y = −4.1 < 0: Quadrant IV.

Q: Q3 (iv). (−2.9, −3.6)

Ans: Both coordinates negative: Quadrant III.

Q: Q3 (v). (−3/5, −1)

Ans: Both coordinates negative: Quadrant III.

Q: Q3 (vi). (2(3/4), −5)

Ans: x > 0, y < 0: Quadrant IV.

Q: Q3 (vii). (−6, √3)

Ans: x < 0, y = √3 > 0: Quadrant II.

Q: Q3 (viii). (−1.49, 2.5)

Ans: x < 0, y > 0: Quadrant II.

Q: Q3 (ix). (9, 0)

Ans: The y-coordinate is 0, so the point lies on the x-axis (in no quadrant).

Q: Q3 (x). (0, −2.5)

Ans: The x-coordinate is 0, so the point lies on the Y-axis (in no quadrant).

Q: Q4 (i). Find the distance between X(−4, −5) and Y(0, 2).

Ans: Distance formula: d = √((x2 − x1)² + (y2 − y1)²)
d = √((0 − (−4))² + (2 − (−5))²) = √(4² + 7²) = √(16 + 49) = √65

Q: Q4 (ii). X(3, 7), Y(−5, 1)

Ans: d = √((−5 − 3)² + (1 − 7)²) = √((−8)² + (−6)²) = √(64 + 36) = √100 = 10

Q: Q4 (iii). X(4, 0), Y(0, 3)

Ans: d = √((0 − 4)² + (3 − 0)²) = √(16 + 9) = √25 = 5

Q: Q4 (iv). X(−1, 9), Y(3, 4)

Ans: d = √((3 − (−1))² + (4 − 9)²) = √(4² + (−5)²) = √(16 + 25) = √41

Q: Q4 (v). X(−7, 2), Y(5, 7)

Ans: d = √((5 − (−7))² + (7 − 2)²) = √(12² + 5²) = √(144 + 25) = √169 = 13

Q: Q4 (vi). X(−4, 12), Y(6, −12)

Ans: d = √((6 − (−4))² + (−12 − 12)²) = √(10² + (−24)²) = √(100 + 576) = √676 = 26

mcqs.q: In the ordered pair (x, y) used for the coordinates of a point, what does the first number represent?
mcqs.why: By definition a point is written as (x, y), where the first entry is the x-coordinate — the horizontal distance from the origin — and the second entry is the y-coordinate. For example, in A(−2, 5), x = −2 and y = 5.

mcqs.q: What are the coordinates of point A in Exercise 10.1 Q1, which is 10 units to the left of the origin and 2 units up?
mcqs.why: Moving left of the origin gives a negative x-coordinate, so x = −10. Moving up gives a positive y-coordinate, so y = 2. Hence the point is A(−10, 2), exactly as read from the figure in the solved exercise.

mcqs.q: Point I(3, 0) in the figure lies on which line?
mcqs.why: The y-coordinate of I is 0. Any point whose y-coordinate is 0 lies on the x-axis, because it has no vertical displacement from the origin. So I(3, 0) lies on the x-axis, 3 units to the right of the origin.

mcqs.q: The point T(0, 9) lies on:
mcqs.why: The x-coordinate of T is 0. Any point whose x-coordinate is 0 lies on the y-axis, because it has no horizontal displacement from the origin. So T(0, 9) lies on the y-axis, 9 units above the origin, and belongs to no quadrant.

mcqs.q: In which quadrant does the point (7, √5) lie?
mcqs.why: Here x = 7 > 0 and y = √5 > 0, so both coordinates are positive. A point with both coordinates positive lies in Quadrant I, so (7, √5) is in Quadrant I.

mcqs.q: In which quadrant does the point (√2, −4.1) lie?
mcqs.why: Here x = √2 > 0 (positive) and y = −4.1 < 0 (negative). Positive x with negative y is the sign pattern of Quadrant IV, so (√2, −4.1) lies in Quadrant IV.

mcqs.q: The point (−2.9, −3.6) lies in:
mcqs.why: Both coordinates are negative: x = −2.9 < 0 and y = −3.6 < 0. The region where both coordinates are negative is Quadrant III, so (−2.9, −3.6) lies in Quadrant III.

mcqs.q: The point (−6, √3) lies in which quadrant?
mcqs.why: Here x = −6 < 0 (negative) while y = √3 > 0 (positive). Negative x with positive y is the sign pattern of Quadrant II, so (−6, √3) lies in Quadrant II.

mcqs.q: The point (9, 0) lies in which quadrant?
options: It lies on the x-axis, in no quadrant
It lies on the y-axis, in no quadrant
mcqs.why: The y-coordinate is 0, so the point sits on the x-axis itself rather than inside any quadrant. Points on the axes belong to no quadrant, so (9, 0) lies on the x-axis, in no quadrant.

mcqs.q: For the point C(6, −7), the x and y coordinates are:
mcqs.why: In the ordered pair (x, y) the first number is x and the second is y. So for C(6, −7): x = 6 and y = −7. The point is plotted 6 units right and 7 units down, in Quadrant IV.

mcqs.q: Which point lies on the y-axis, 3 units below the origin?
mcqs.why: A point on the y-axis must have x-coordinate 0, and being below the origin means a negative y-coordinate. E(0, −3) has x = 0 and y = −3, so it lies on the y-axis, 3 units below the origin.

mcqs.q: Find the distance between X(−4, −5) and Y(0, 2).
mcqs.why: Distance formula: d = √((x2 − x1)² + (y2 − y1)²). Substituting: d = √((0 − (−4))² + (2 − (−5))²) = √(4² + 7²) = √(16 + 49) = √65. So the distance is √65 units.

mcqs.q: Find the distance between X(3, 7) and Y(−5, 1).
mcqs.why: Distance formula: d = √((x2 − x1)² + (y2 − y1)²). Substituting: d = √((−5 − 3)² + (1 − 7)²) = √((−8)² + (−6)²) = √(64 + 36) = √100 = 10. So the distance is 10 units.

mcqs.q: Find the distance between X(−7, 2) and Y(5, 7).
mcqs.why: Distance formula: d = √((x2 − x1)² + (y2 − y1)²). Substituting: d = √((5 − (−7))² + (7 − 2)²) = √(12² + 5²) = √(144 + 25) = √169 = 13. So the distance is 13 units.

mcqs.q: Find the distance between X(−4, 12) and Y(6, −12).
mcqs.why: Distance formula: d = √((x2 − x1)² + (y2 − y1)²). Substituting: d = √((6 − (−4))² + (−12 − 12)²) = √(10² + (−24)²) = √(100 + 576) = √676 = 26. So the distance is 26 units.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.2
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Points that lie on the same straight line are called collinear points; points not on one straight line are non-collinear.
  • Three points are collinear if the sum of the distances between two pairs equals the distance between the extreme pair, e.g. d(p, q) + d(q, r) = d(p, r).
  • For p(5, −2), q(1, 2), r(−2, 5): d(p, q) = 4√2, d(q, r) = 3√2 and d(p, r) = 7√2, and 4√2 + 3√2 = 7√2, so the points are collinear.
  • For A(−3, −4), B(0, 2), C(2, 6): d(A, B) = 3√5, d(B, C) = 2√5, d(A, C) = 5√5, and 3√5 + 2√5 = 5√5, so they are collinear.
  • Four points A(−9, −5), B(−3, −2), C(3, 1), D(9, 4) are collinear because d(A, B) = d(B, C) = d(C, D) = 3√5 and their sum 9√5 equals d(A, D) = 9√5.
  • In a figure, points are non-collinear when at least one of them does not lie on the line through the others, e.g. (E, F, G) and (M, N, O) in Q1.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1 (i). Use the figure to indicate whether the points (O, G, I) are collinear or non-collinear.

Ans: In the figure, O, G and I all lie on the same straight line (the line through A, O, G, I), so they are collinear.

Q: Q1 (ii). (E, F, G)

Ans: F and E lie on the slanted line through B, O, P, but G does not lie on that line, so (E, F, G) are non-collinear.

Q: Q1 (iii). (M, N, O)

Ans: M and N lie on the vertical line through H, I, J, but O does not lie on it, so (M, N, O) are non-collinear.

Q: Q1 (iv). (F, B, O)

Ans: F, B and O all lie on the same slanted line (through F, B, O, P, E, D), so they are collinear.

Q: Q1 (v). (E, K, J)

Ans: E, K and J all lie on the same line (through C, E, K, J), so they are collinear.

Q: Q1 (vi). (J, G, B)

Ans: J, G and B all lie on the same diagonal line (through B, G, J), so they are collinear.

Q: Q1 (vii). (A, O, P)

Ans: A and O lie on one line and A and P on another; the three points do not lie on a single straight line, so (A, O, P) are non-collinear.

Q: Q1 (viii). (C, D, L)

Ans: C, D and L all lie on the same line (through C, D, L, M), so they are collinear.

Q: Q1 (ix). (H, I, J)

Ans: H, I and J all lie on the same vertical line (through H, I, J, M, N), so they are collinear.

Q: Q1 (x). (B, C, D)

Ans: B lies on the slanted line through F, O, P, E, D, while C and D lie on the bottom line; the three are not on one line, so (B, C, D) are non-collinear.

Q: Q2. Show that the points p(5, −2), q(1, 2) and r(−2, 5) are collinear.

Ans: Using the distance formula d = √((x2 − x1)² + (y2 − y1)²):
d(p, q) = √((1 − 5)² + (2 − (−2))²) = √(16 + 16) = √32 = 4√2
d(q, r) = √((−2 − 1)² + (5 − 2)²) = √(9 + 9) = √18 = 3√2
d(p, r) = √((−2 − 5)² + (5 − (−2))²) = √(49 + 49) = √98 = 7√2
Since d(p, q) + d(q, r) = 4√2 + 3√2 = 7√2 = d(p, r), the points are collinear.

Q: Q3. Show that the points A(−3, −4), B(0, 2) and C(2, 6) are collinear.

Ans: d(A, B) = √((0 − (−3))² + (2 − (−4))²) = √(9 + 36) = √45 = 3√5
d(B, C) = √((2 − 0)² + (6 − 2)²) = √(4 + 16) = √20 = 2√5
d(A, C) = √((2 − (−3))² + (6 − (−4))²) = √(25 + 100) = √125 = 5√5
Since d(A, B) + d(B, C) = 3√5 + 2√5 = 5√5 = d(A, C), the points are collinear.

Q: Q4. Show that the points A(−9, −5), B(−3, −2), C(3, 1) and D(9, 4) are collinear.

Ans: d(A, B) = √((−3 − (−9))² + (−2 − (−5))²) = √(36 + 9) = √45 = 3√5
d(B, C) = √((3 − (−3))² + (1 − (−2))²) = √(36 + 9) = √45 = 3√5
d(C, D) = √((9 − 3)² + (4 − 1)²) = √(36 + 9) = √45 = 3√5
d(A, D) = √((9 − (−9))² + (4 − (−5))²) = √(324 + 81) = √405 = 9√5
Since d(A, B) + d(B, C) + d(C, D) = 3√5 + 3√5 + 3√5 = 9√5 = d(A, D), the four points are collinear.

mcqs.q: Points that lie on the same straight line are called:
mcqs.why: By definition, points lying on one and the same straight line are collinear points. In Exercise 10.2 Q1, for example, O, G and I lie on the same straight line, so they are collinear.

mcqs.q: Using the figure in Q1, the points (O, G, I) are:
mcqs.why: In the figure, O, G and I all lie on the same straight line (the line through A, O, G, I). Points on a single straight line are collinear, so (O, G, I) are collinear.

mcqs.q: Using the figure in Q1, the points (E, F, G) are:
options: On the vertical line through H and I
mcqs.why: F and E lie on the slanted line through B, O and P, but G does not lie on that line. Since the three points do not lie on one straight line, (E, F, G) are non-collinear.

mcqs.q: Using the figure in Q1, the points (H, I, J) are:
mcqs.why: H, I and J all lie on the same vertical line (the line through H, I, J, M, N). Points on a single straight line are collinear, so (H, I, J) are collinear.

mcqs.q: Using the figure in Q1, the points (A, O, P) are:
options: On the line through C, D, L
mcqs.why: A and O lie on one line and A and P lie on another line; the three points do not lie on a single straight line. Therefore (A, O, P) are non-collinear.

mcqs.q: Three points P, Q, R are collinear (with Q between P and R) if:
options: d(P, Q) + d(Q, R) = d(P, R)
d(P, Q) × d(Q, R) = d(P, R)
d(P, Q) + d(Q, R) < d(P, R)
mcqs.why: If Q lies on the straight segment PR, the two smaller distances add up exactly to the whole distance: d(P, Q) + d(Q, R) = d(P, R). This is the distance test used throughout Exercise 10.2 to prove collinearity.

mcqs.q: For p(5, −2) and q(1, 2), the distance d(p, q) is:
For q(1, 2) and r(−2, 5), the distance d(q, r) is:
The points p(5, −2), q(1, 2) and r(−2, 5) are collinear because:
options: d(p, q) = d(q, r) = d(p, r)
d(p, q) + d(p, r) = d(q, r)
d(p, r) is the smallest distance

mcqs.q: For A(−3, −4), B(0, 2) and C(2, 6), which statement proves the points are collinear?
options: d(A, B) = d(B, C) = d(A, C)
d(A, C) + d(B, C) = d(A, B)
d(A, B) + d(B, C) > d(A, C)

lessons.title: Exercise 10.3
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Three points form an equilateral triangle when all three sides are equal: |AB| = |BC| = |CA|, found with the distance formula.
  • Three points form an isosceles triangle when exactly two sides are equal, e.g. |BC| = |CA| ≠ |AB|.
  • Three points form a scalene triangle when all three sides are different: |AB| ≠ |BC| ≠ |CA|.
  • Three points form a right angled triangle when the sides satisfy Pythagoras' theorem: the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides.
  • Example (equilateral): (5, 8), (5, 12), (5 + 2√3, 10) all give side length 4.
  • Example (right angled): (−2, 3), (4, 3), (−2, 11) give sides 6, 10, 8 and 6² + 8² = 100 = 10², so the triangle is right angled at A.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1 (i). Use distance formula to show that the points (5, 8), (5, 12), (5 + 2√3, 10) develop an equilateral triangle.

Ans: Let the points be A(5, 8), B(5, 12), C(5 + 2√3, 10). Using d = √((x2 − x1)² + (y2 − y1)²):
|AB| = √(0² + 4²) = 4
|BC| = √((2√3)² + (−2)²) = √(12 + 4) = 4
|CA| = √((−2√3)² + 2²) = √(12 + 4) = 4
|AB| = |BC| = |CA|, so the points develop an equilateral triangle.

Q: Q1 (ii). (0, 8), (0, −8), (8√3, 0)

Ans: |AB| = √(0² + (−16)²) = 16
|BC| = √((8√3)² + 8²) = √(192 + 64) = √256 = 16
|CA| = √((−8√3)² + (−8)²) = √(192 + 64) = 16
All three sides are equal, so the points develop an equilateral triangle.

Q: Q1 (iii). (−6, 0), (10, 0), (2, 8√3)

Ans: |AB| = √(16² + 0²) = 16
|BC| = √((−8)² + (8√3)²) = √(64 + 192) = 16
|CA| = √(8² + (−8√3)²) = √(64 + 192) = 16
All three sides are equal, so the points develop an equilateral triangle.

Q: Q1 (iv). (−3, −2), (−3, 4), (−3 + 3√3, 1)

Ans: |AB| = √(0² + 6²) = 6
|BC| = √((3√3)² + (−3)²) = √(27 + 9) = 6
|CA| = √((−3√3)² + 3²) = √(27 + 9) = 6
All three sides are equal, so the points develop an equilateral triangle.

Q: Q2 (i). Use distance formula to show that the points (−1, 6), (3, 2), (6, 9) are the vertices of an isosceles triangle.

Ans: Let A(−1, 6), B(3, 2), C(6, 9).
|AB| = √(4² + (−4)²) = √32
|BC| = √(3² + 7²) = √58
|CA| = √(7² + 3²) = √58
|BC| = |CA|, so two sides are equal and the points are the vertices of an isosceles triangle.

Q: Q2 (ii). (4, 7), (5, 0), (−3, 8)

Ans: |AB| = √(1² + (−7)²) = √50
|BC| = √((−8)² + 8²) = √128
|CA| = √((−7)² + 1²) = √50
|AB| = |CA|, so the points are the vertices of an isosceles triangle.

Q: Q2 (iii). (−4, 6), (4, −2), (5, 7)

Ans: |AB| = √(8² + (−8)²) = √128
|BC| = √(1² + 9²) = √82
|CA| = √(9² + 1²) = √82
|BC| = |CA|, so the points are the vertices of an isosceles triangle.

Q: Q2 (iv). (0, 6), (4, 2), (7, 9)

Ans: |AB| = √(4² + (−4)²) = √32
|BC| = √(3² + 7²) = √58
|CA| = √(7² + 3²) = √58
|BC| = |CA|, so the points are the vertices of an isosceles triangle.

Q: Q3 (i). Use distance formula to show that the points (−2, 5), (4, 3), (7, −5) represent a scalene triangle.

Ans: Let A(−2, 5), B(4, 3), C(7, −5).
|AB| = √(6² + (−2)²) = √40
|BC| = √(3² + (−8)²) = √73
|CA| = √(9² + (−10)²) = √181
All three sides are different (|AB| ≠ |BC| ≠ |CA|), so the points represent a scalene triangle.

Q: Q3 (ii). (2, 1), (6, 1), (5, 5)

Ans: |AB| = √(4² + 0²) = 4
|BC| = √((−1)² + 4²) = √17
|CA| = √(3² + 4²) = 5
All three sides are different, so the points represent a scalene triangle.

Q: Q3 (iii). (−5, −4), (2, 3), (−2, 4)

Ans: |AB| = √(7² + 7²) = √98
|BC| = √((−4)² + 1²) = √17
|CA| = √(3² + 8²) = √73
All three sides are different, so the points represent a scalene triangle.

Q: Q3 (iv). (−10, 4), (7, 1), (−3, −3)

Ans: |AB| = √(17² + (−3)²) = √298
|BC| = √((−10)² + (−4)²) = √116
|CA| = √(7² + 7²) = √98
All three sides are different, so the points represent a scalene triangle.

Q: Q4 (i). Use distance formula to show that the points (−2, 3), (4, 3), (−2, 11) form a right angled triangle.

Ans: Let A(−2, 3), B(4, 3), C(−2, 11).
|AB| = 6, |BC| = √(36 + 64) = 10, |CA| = 8
Check by Pythagoras theorem: |AB|² + |CA|² = 36 + 64 = 100 = |BC|²
So the points form a right angled triangle (right angle at A).

Q: Q4 (ii). (1, 4), (1, 7), (8, 4)

Ans: |AB| = 3, |BC| = √(49 + 9) = √58, |CA| = 7
|AB|² + |CA|² = 9 + 49 = 58 = |BC|²
So the points form a right angled triangle.

Q: Q4 (iii). (−6, 5), (−6, −7), (−1, −7)

Ans: |AB| = 12, |BC| = 5, |CA| = √(25 + 144) = 13
|AB|² + |BC|² = 144 + 25 = 169 = |CA|²
So the points form a right angled triangle.

Q: Q4 (iv). (1, 4), (3, 2), (6, 9)

Ans: |AB| = √(4 + 4) = √8, |BC| = √(9 + 49) = √58, |CA| = √(25 + 25) = √50
|AB|² + |CA|² = 8 + 50 = 58 = |BC|²
So the points form a right angled triangle.

mcqs.q: Three points A, B, C form an equilateral triangle if:
options: One side squared equals the sum of the squares of the other two
mcqs.why: An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal. In Exercise 10.3 Q1 each triple is checked with the distance formula and accepted as equilateral only when |AB| = |BC| = |CA|.

mcqs.q: For the points (5, 8), (5, 12) and (5 + 2√3, 10), the side |AB| between (5, 8) and (5, 12) is:
The points (0, 8), (0, −8) and (8√3, 0) form an equilateral triangle because each side equals:
Three points form an isosceles triangle if:
mcqs.why: An isosceles triangle has exactly two equal sides. For example, for (−1, 6), (3, 2), (6, 9): |AB| = √32, |BC| = √58 and |CA| = √58, so |BC| = |CA| and the triangle is isosceles.

mcqs.q: For A(−1, 6), B(3, 2) and C(6, 9), the equal sides are:
For the points (4, 7), (5, 0) and (−3, 8), the side lengths are:
Three points form a scalene triangle if:
options: The square of one side equals the sum of the squares of the other two
mcqs.why: A scalene triangle has all three sides of different lengths. For example, (−2, 5), (4, 3), (7, −5) give |AB| = √40, |BC| = √73 and |CA| = √181 — all different, so the triangle is scalene.

mcqs.q: For the points (2, 1), (6, 1) and (5, 5), the triangle is scalene because the sides are:
mcqs.why: Working: |AB| = √((6 − 2)² + (1 − 1)²) = √(16 + 0) = 4. |BC| = √((5 − 6)² + (5 − 1)²) = √(1 + 16) = √17. |CA| = √((2 − 5)² + (1 − 5)²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. The sides 4, √17 and 5 are all different, so the triangle is scalene.

mcqs.q: Three points form a right angled triangle if the sides satisfy:
options: Pythagoras' theorem: the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides
mcqs.why: A triangle is right angled exactly when Pythagoras' theorem holds for its sides: (longest side)² = (side 1)² + (side 2)². This is the test applied to every triple in Exercise 10.3 Q4.

mcqs.q: The points (−2, 3), (4, 3) and (−2, 11) form a right angled triangle because:
mcqs.why: Working: |AB| = distance between (−2, 3) and (4, 3) = √(6² + 0²) = 6. |BC| = √((−2 − 4)² + (11 − 3)²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10. |CA| = √((−2 + 2)² + (3 − 11)²) = √(0 + 64) = 8. Check: |AB|² + |CA|² = 36 + 64 = 100 = |BC|², so by Pythagoras' theorem the triangle is right angled (at A).

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Coordinate Geometry is also called Analytic Geometry, and the coordinate plane is a two-dimensional plane.
  • On the x-axis, points to the right of the origin represent positive real numbers; on the y-axis, points below the origin are associated with negative real numbers.
  • The point (4, −3) lies in Quadrant IV (x positive, y negative), not Quadrant III; (−6, −8) lies in Quadrant III.
  • In Quadrant II the x-coordinate is negative (and the y-coordinate is positive).
  • The point (0, −4) lies on the y-axis, since its x-coordinate is 0.
  • The distance between (6, 0) and (0, 8) is 10, from √((0 − 6)² + (8 − 0)²) = √(36 + 64) = √100.
  • Three collinear points do NOT form a triangle; non-collinear points with |XY| + |YZ| > |XZ| form a triangle.
  • In triangle ABC, |AB| = |BC| alone makes it isosceles, not equilateral; a right angle at A means |BC|² = |AB|² + |AC|².

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1 (i). Coordinate Geometry is also called Analytic Geometry.

Ans: True

Q: Q1 (ii). Coordinate plane represents a two dimensional plane.

Ans: True

Q: Q1 (iii). On x-axis, points to the right of the origin represent positive real number.

Ans: True

Q: Q1 (iv). Point (4, −3) lies in quadrant III. (It lies in quadrant IV.)

Ans: False

Q: Q1 (v). Distance between (6, 0) and (0, 8) is 10.

Ans: True

Q: Q1 (vi). Three collinear points form a triangle.

Ans: False

Q: Q1 (vii). In a triangle ABC, if |AB| = |BC| then the triangle is an equilateral one. (It is an isosceles triangle.)

Ans: False

Q: Q2 (i). (−6, −8) lies in quadrant ____.

Ans: III

Q: Q2 (ii). On y-axis, the points below the origin are associated with ____ real numbers.

Ans: negative

Q: Q2 (iii). In quadrant II, x-coordinate is ____.

Ans: negative

Q: Q2 (iv). Point (0, −4) lies on ____.

Ans: y-axis

Q: Q3 (i). In which quadrant, the x-coordinate is positive and the y-coordinate is negative?

Options: (a) Quadrant IV (b) Quadrant III (c) Quadrant II (d) Quadrant I

Correct answer: Quadrant IV

Q: Q3 (ii). In which quadrant the point (−7, 5) lies?

Options: (a) Quadrant I (b) Quadrant II (c) Quadrant III (d) Quadrant IV

Correct answer: Quadrant II

Q: Q3 (iii). Three non-collinear points A, B and C form an isosceles triangle if:

Options: (a) d(A, B) = d(A, C) (b) d(A, C) = d(B, A) (c) d(C, A) = d(C, B) (d) All are true

Correct answer: All are true

Q: Q3 (iv). For a triangle ABC, with right angle at A, which of the following is true?

Options: (a) |AB|² = |AC|² + |BC|² (b) |AC|² = |AB|² + |BC|² (c) |BC|² = |AB|² + |AC|² (d) All are true

Correct answer: |BC|² = |AB|² + |AC|²

Q: Q3 (v). For the points X, Y and Z, |XY| + |YZ| > |XZ| shows that:

Options: (a) X, Y, Z are collinear (b) X, Y, Z are non collinear (c) XYZ is a triangle (d) Both (b) and (c) are true

Correct answer: Both (b) and (c) are true

mcqs.q: Coordinate Geometry is also called:
mcqs.why: Revision Exercise Q1(i) is True: Coordinate Geometry, the study of geometry using coordinates and algebra, is also known as Analytic Geometry.

mcqs.q: The coordinate plane represents a:
mcqs.why: Revision Exercise Q1(ii) is True: the coordinate plane, formed by the x-axis and y-axis, represents a two dimensional plane in which every point is fixed by an ordered pair (x, y).

mcqs.q: On the x-axis, points to the right of the origin represent:
mcqs.why: Revision Exercise Q1(iii) is True: moving right from the origin along the x-axis increases the x-coordinate through positive values, so points to the right of the origin represent positive real numbers.

mcqs.q: The point (4, −3) lies in:
mcqs.why: Here x = 4 > 0 and y = −3 < 0. Positive x with negative y is Quadrant IV. (Revision Q1(iv), which claimed Quadrant III, is False — Quadrant III needs both coordinates negative.)

mcqs.q: The distance between (6, 0) and (0, 8) is:
mcqs.why: Distance formula: d = √((x2 − x1)² + (y2 − y1)²). Substituting: d = √((0 − 6)² + (8 − 0)²) = √((−6)² + 8²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10. So the distance is 10 units, and Revision Q1(v) is True.

mcqs.q: Three collinear points form a triangle. This statement is:
options: True, if the points are far apart
False — collinear points lie on one line and cannot form a triangle
mcqs.why: Revision Q1(vi) is False. Collinear points all lie on a single straight line, so the 'triangle' collapses to a line segment with zero area. Only three non-collinear points can form a triangle.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, if |AB| = |BC| then the triangle is:
mcqs.why: Revision Q1(vii) is False as printed (it claimed equilateral). Having exactly two equal sides, |AB| = |BC|, is the definition of an isosceles triangle. An equilateral triangle needs all three sides equal: |AB| = |BC| = |CA|.

mcqs.q: The point (−6, −8) lies in quadrant:
mcqs.why: Both coordinates are negative: x = −6 < 0 and y = −8 < 0. The region with both coordinates negative is Quadrant III, which is the book's fill-in-the-blank answer for (−6, −8).

mcqs.q: In Quadrant II, the x-coordinate is:
mcqs.why: Quadrant II is the region to the left of the y-axis and above the x-axis, so every point there has a negative x-coordinate and a positive y-coordinate. This is the book's fill-in-the-blank answer for Q2(iii).

mcqs.q: For the points X, Y and Z, |XY| + |YZ| > |XZ| shows that:
options: X, Y, Z are non-collinear and XYZ is a triangle
X, Y, Z lie on the x-axis
mcqs.why: If the points were collinear, the two shorter distances would add up exactly to the longest: |XY| + |YZ| = |XZ|. The strict inequality |XY| + |YZ| > |XZ| (the triangle inequality) means Y is off the line XZ, so X, Y, Z are non-collinear and form a triangle. This combines the book's keyed options (b) and (c) into one explicit option.
